title: Calibration of systematic distortions in quantum emitter localization microscopy for deterministic nanophotonic fabrication
authors: Chenxi Ma, Maximilian Heller, Timon Handrup, Yiteng Zhang, Tobias M. Krieger, Thomas Oberleitner, Zenghui Jiang, Xian Zheng, Eddy P. Rugeramigabo, Folke Dencker, Armando Rastelli, Fei Ding, Michael Zopf
abstract: Quantum photonic technologies greatly benefit from quantum light emitters with high brightness, indistinguishability, and reliable polarization characteristics. Achieving optimal performance relies on the accurate localization of emitters and their deterministic integration into tailored photonic structures with nanometer-scale accuracy. Although marker-based photoluminescence imaging techniques can achieve statistical fitting uncertainties below 10 nm, the ultimate integration yield is often limited by uncorrected systematic distortions in custom cryo-optical setups that compromise metrological accuracy. Here, we present an in situ calibration protocol that uses lithographically defined gold nanodisk arrays as references to calibrate optical distortions with a Zernike vector-field model. On held-out validation patterns beyond the calibration dataset, this correction reduces the residual systematic bias to 5.3 nm with a 2D scatter of 24.6 nm across the analyzed field of view. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying this correction to the deterministic fabrication of circular mesa structures around semiconductor quantum dots reduces the variance in emission polarization by 49%, indicating improved registration accuracy. This calibration strategy offers a practical route to high-yield deterministic integration of quantum emitters into scalable quantum photonic circuits.
summary: This paper presents an advanced calibration protocol to correct systematic optical distortions in complex, custom cryo-optical setups used for localizing quantum emitters. By modeling these distortions using a Zernike vector-field approach and validating it with nanodisk arrays, the authors significantly improved absolute positioning accuracy. This method offers a practical pathway to deterministically integrating quantum light sources into scalable photonic circuits.
main_problem: The ultimate integration yield of quantum emitters into photonic structures is limited by uncorrected systematic optical distortions inherent in custom cryo-optical setups, even when statistical localization uncertainty is low.
main_result: An *in situ* calibration protocol using a Zernike vector-field model reduced the residual systematic bias to 5.3 nm and improved emission polarization variance by 49% upon application to deterministic fabrication.
method: The authors developed an in situ metrological calibration framework that models field-dependent coordinate offsets using a Zernike polynomial expansion, applied to lithographically defined reference arrays.
model_or_system: The experiment uses quantum emitter localization microscopy on semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) within custom cryo-optical setups. The systematic distortions are modeled mathematically using the Zernike vector-field model for correction.
key_observables: Residual systematic bias (reduced to 5.3 nm), polarization variance reduction (49%), and localization repeatability ($\sigma$).
important_parameters: Nanometer-scale accuracy, cryogenic temperature (4 K), Zernike polynomial order ($n=10$), and the use of lithographically defined gold nanodisk arrays as references.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation addressed is uncorrected systematic optical distortions; one assumption involves approximating the QD emission source for simulation purposes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup schematic, performance metrics comparing localization uncertainties (QD vs. nanodisks), and validation showing the reduction of systematic offsets after applying the Zernike correction model.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of systematic distortion limiting integration yield, details the use of a Zernike vector-field model calibrated with reference arrays, presents quantitative results showing bias reduction and polarization improvement, and concludes by establishing the method's utility for scalable quantum photonic circuits.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to experimental quantum optics and open quantum systems as it provides a critical metrological tool necessary to translate high-precision statistical measurements into reliable absolute positioning required for building functional quantum devices.
